key_insight: In strongly stratified horizontally sheared flows, turbulence can arise through two distinct routes, but both ultimately generate vertical shear and small-scale Kelvin–Helmholtz mixing when the buoyancy Reynolds number is sufficiently large.
engineering_relevance: This identifies when horizontally sheared stratified systems can still produce significant diapycnal mixing, which matters for predicting mixing efficiency in geophysical and engineering flows with weak or absent initial vertical shear.
method: Linear stability analysis of horizontally sheared stratified flow with no initial vertical shear
Direct numerical simulations to track nonlinear evolution and turbulence onset
Comparison of two instability pathways: vertically modulated modes versus columnar vortical evolution
evidence_signal: The abstract reports combined linear theory and DNS showing two turbulence pathways and comparing the resulting vertical scales and peak mixing efficiencies across sufficiently large buoyancy Reynolds number conditions.
watch_item: The mixing pathway and efficiency depend on vertical-scale selection and on reaching sufficiently large Re_b, so conclusions may not transfer to lower-Re_b regimes or flows with different stratification and boundary conditions.
paper_title: Two pathways to diapycnal mixing in strongly stratified flows with no initial vertical shear
